scenes.narration: four hundred and twenty-eight billion dollars. By our own estimate, that is about how much stock market value Nvidia, the company whose chips power artificial intelligence, lost in just two trading days in November twenty twenty-six.

No factory burned down. No chip stopped working. No customer cancelled an order. What changed over one weekend was a story about one man, and about where some of the world's most wanted chips may end up.
So how can a single story wipe out that much value so fast? And why does a small city state in Southeast Asia keep turning up in Nvidia's numbers?

By the end of this video, you will know why investors treat Nvidia's founder as part of the product, what the reports actually claim and what is only alleged, how American export rules try to keep the best chips out of China, and what happens next.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the company. Nvidia designs the processors that train and run most of today's artificial intelligence. In its fiscal year that ended in January twenty twenty-six, it reported about two hundred and sixteen billion dollars of revenue. Before that weekend, its shares were worth about four and a half trillion dollars, by our estimate from its share count.

Its founder and chief executive is Jensen Huang. Investors do not just see him as a manager. They see him as part of the product. One well known chip analyst, Stacy Rasgon, put it in five words to CNBC. Jensen is Nvidia. Nvidia is Jensen.

Companies have a name for this. It is called key person risk. Nvidia's own annual report warns that it is highly dependent on the services of its longstanding executive team, and that failing to plan for succession could hurt its long term success. The report does not name him. And the latest proxy statement does not use the word succession even once.

Huang also owns a slice of the company, about three point six percent of the shares according to that proxy, roughly eight hundred and seventy million shares. By our estimate, that stake lost about fifteen billion dollars of paper value in those two days, assuming his holding has not changed since March.

Let me draw key person risk. Here is the company, with its chips, its software and its customers. Here is the founder, who sets the strategy and sells the vision. Now draw an arrow between them. When investors believe that arrow carries the whole company, the founder's reputation becomes part of the share price. One analyst, Dan Ives, said that without Huang, Nvidia would be worth twenty five to thirty percent less. That is an opinion, not a fact. But it shows how thick that arrow is.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Then, over one weekend in November, that arrow came under strain.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: On October twenty-ninth, the New York Times reported on a relationship between Huang and a businesswoman linked to Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud company that buys Nvidia chips. Then, on Friday, November sixth, according to reporting relayed by Bloomberg, the Times reported that American intelligence officials had told the administration that she was working for China's Ministry of State Security.

On Sunday, November eighth, Huang wrote to Nvidia's employees. In his own words, I was unfaithful to my wife. There is no excuse for what I did. That is all this video will say about his private life. What matters for the money is what came next.

The same day, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation, in light of reporting that its founder had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it had no reason to believe that national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised, and that it had confidence in Huang. China's foreign ministry called the spy allegation unsubstantiated. And no one has been charged with anything.

On Monday, the market answered. The S and P five hundred rose more than two percent. Rival chip makers soared. A M D jumped about thirteen percent, and Broadcom almost nine. Nvidia fell more than four percent. When a company drops on a day its whole industry rises, investors are reacting to that company alone.

On Tuesday, the independent directors named their investigator, Joon Kim, a former acting United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, with the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz. The stock fell again, by about five and a half percent, to just under one hundred and sixty-nine dollars a share.

Put the two days together and the shares lost about nine and a half percent. With roughly twenty-four billion shares outstanding, that is about four hundred and twenty-eight billion dollars of market value, gone, by our estimate.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So why would a story about one person and one customer frighten investors this much? The answer is China, and the rules that keep Nvidia's best chips out of it.

keyframes.label: China, and the rules on chips

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Since twenty twenty-two, the United States has required licences to export Nvidia's most advanced chips to China. In October twenty twenty-three, the rules got tighter and covered a long list of products. In April twenty twenty-five, even its H twenty chip needed a licence, and Nvidia took a charge of about four and a half billion dollars in that quarter.

Nvidia now says it is effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center market. In its most recent reported quarter, shipments of its Hopper data center chips to China were less than one percent of data center revenue. Customers headquartered in China still made up about eight percent of total revenue, by our calculation from the filing.

Where there are strict rules and high prices, some people try to get around them. The Justice Department has brought several chip export cases. In one, a businessman and his company pleaded guilty in a case involving at least one hundred and sixty million dollars of Nvidia chips, which prosecutors said had been relabeled. And in October twenty twenty-six, a California man was indicted over servers allegedly sent through Malaysia and Singapore. Nvidia is not accused in any of these cases.

Let me draw the route these cases describe. Here is the chip, sold to a company in a third country. Here is a middleman, often in Southeast Asia. And here is the arrow the rules forbid, from the middleman into China. The export rules sit on that last arrow like a checkpoint. Prosecutors say smugglers try to slip past it with false paperwork and new labels.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Which brings us to Singapore, and to the customer at the center of this story.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Here is a number that has puzzled many investors. In Nvidia's twenty twenty-five fiscal year, Singapore accounted for eighteen percent of its revenue, based on where customers were billed. That was more than twenty-three billion dollars. But in the same report, Nvidia explained that customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing, and that its products are almost always shipped elsewhere. Actual shipments to Singapore were less than two percent of revenue.

Let me draw that gap. Here is the bar for billing, eighteen percent. Here is the bar for what was actually shipped there, less than two. According to Nvidia, the difference is invoicing, not shipping. The company later said that over ninety-nine percent of its controlled data center revenue billed to Singapore came from orders by companies based in the United States.

scenes.narration: Megaspeed is one of the companies that buy Nvidia chips in the region. According to a Reuters factbox, it took the name Megaspeed in twenty twenty-three, and its assets grew from thirty-three million dollars to three billion dollars in a single year. The New York Times reported in twenty twenty-five that it had bought nearly two billion dollars worth of Nvidia's most advanced products through a Malaysian subsidiary.

That year, Senator Tom Cotton asked the Commerce Department to investigate Megaspeed, alleging that American chips were being diverted to China through a network of shell companies. According to the New York Times, a Commerce inquiry was later paused after Nvidia's general counsel contacted the investigators, and the case moved to the Justice Department. The Commerce Department says it handled the case by the book.

scenes.narration: Megaspeed calls the reporting misleading, and says regulators and Nvidia found no evidence of any illegal transfer of chips. It has not been charged, and it is not on the government's trade blacklist. Nvidia has described Megaspeed as a small commercial cloud, and says the diversion claims were thoroughly investigated and debunked.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So, with all of that unresolved, what happens now?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: First, the investigation. A committee of independent directors, helped by outside lawyers, will examine all available information, and the board has promised further updates. Until it reports, investors are pricing a question mark.

Second, the calendar. Nvidia is scheduled to report its quarterly results on November seventeenth. And three House committee chairmen have asked Huang to brief them behind closed doors on November eighteenth, saying it is vital that Congress determines the extent to which national security has been placed at risk. It is not yet confirmed that the briefing will happen.

Third, politics. President Trump has publicly backed Huang. He said Huang told him he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy, and that he really believes him. That is his account.

So why did Nvidia lose about four hundred and twenty-eight billion dollars in two days? Not because its chips got worse. Because investors suddenly had to price two risks at once. The first is the risk of depending on one person. The second is the risk that the rules around its most valuable product could bite harder than anyone expected. Neither risk has been shown to have caused any harm. The board says it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised, and nobody has been charged. But markets do not wait for verdicts. They price stories, and they price people. Even a company worth about four trillion dollars can hang on one name, one weekend, and one question.
